data.title: Stocks to watch: Tata Steel, Waaree, Adani Energy, Maruti, IndusInd Bank
data.description:
Stocks to watch today: GIFT Nifty indicated a positive start for domestic indices on Monday as it traded 167.5 points, or 0.65 per cent, lower at 25,913 as of 07:42 AM.
 
Earlier on Friday, the Nifty 50 index closed 26.30 points, or 1.12 per cent, higher at 25,800.60. The 30-share BSE Sensex rallied 897.96 points, or 1.08 per cent, to settle at 83,919.71.
 
Meanwhile, Asian stocks were trading mixed, defying Friday’s moves on Wall Street. At the last check, South Korea's Kospi index was down 4.25 per cent, while Japan's Nikkei 225 was up 4.59 per cent. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 traded 0.08 per cent higher.
 
 
Overnight in the US, all three key Wall Street indices closed sharply lower. The Dow Jones Industrial Average tanked 1.93 per cent, the S&P 500 lost 3.7 per cent, and the Nasdaq Composite plummeted 5.28 per cent.
 
Oil prices stayed below $95 per barrel. Brent crude’s December futures were quoting at $92.29, down 0.30 per cent. WTI crude fell 0.22 per cent to $83.23 per barrel.
 
Stocks to watch
 
Tata Steel: The company has approved the sale of its tubes business and entire stake in Tata Steel Colours to APL Apollo Tubes in transactions valued at up to ₹28,000 crore, subject to regulatory clearances, with completion expected by March 2028. Waaree Energies: Its wholly owned subsidiary, Waaree Forever Energies, has signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with SECI for a 700 MW solar project in Solapur, Maharashtra. The project also includes a 700 MW/2,800 MWh battery energy storage system (BESS).
 
Adani Energy Solutions: Subsidiary Powerpulse Trading Solutions has received a Letter of Award from WBSEDCL to supply 1,750 MW of round-the-clock renewable energy, along with an additional 750 MW under a greenshoe option.
 
Maruti Suzuki: The company has announced price hikes across select models with immediate effect. The weighted average increase is around 0.31 per cent to partially offset sustained input cost pressures.
 
IndusInd Bank: The bank’s board has decided to terminate former MD and CEO Sumant Kathpalia’s employment with immediate effect following an enquiry. It has also invoked applicable malus and clawback provisions retrospectively from March 24, 2020.
 
Premier Explosives: The company has secured an international export order worth $33.60 million (around ₹311 crore) for the manufacturing and supply of defence explosives.
 
RVNL: The company has emerged as the lowest bidder (L1) for a ₹348.49 crore East Coast Railway order to augment the Vadlapudi Wagon Workshop in Visakhapatnam.
 
Ratnaveer Precision Engineering: The company has secured long-term orders covering nearly 50 per cent of its upcoming copper clad laminate (CCL) manufacturing capacity. Its ₹338 crore capex project targets ₹750 crore in annual revenue and ₹150 crore in EBITDA at full capacity, with commercial production expected from February 2027.
 
Texmaco Rail & Engineering: The company has received two domestic letters of intent worth a combined ₹230.58 crore from JSW Group entities for manufacturing and supplying 553 wagons.
 
Aurobindo Pharma: The USFDA has issued an Establishment Inspection Report (EIR) with a Voluntary Action Indicated (VAI) classification for subsidiary Apitoria Pharma’s API facility, formally closing the August 2026 inspection that had resulted in three observations.
 
Cohance Lifesciences: The USFDA has issued an EIR with a VAI classification for its formulation manufacturing facility in Shamshabad, Telangana, formally concluding the earlier inspection.
 
Welspun Living: The company’s board has approved capital expenditure of up to ₹3,200 crore through its subsidiary, Welspun Home Solutions.
 
Arvind: The company has partnered with unspun to become the first manufacturer to deploy its OneWeave 3D weaving technology.
 
NATCO Pharma: The USFDA inspection at its Kothur facility in Hyderabad has concluded with seven Form 483 observations.

data.title: 26,000 next milestone for Nifty; Fortis among 3 stock ideas: Osho Krishan
data.description:
Disclaimer: This article is written by Osho Krishan, Chief Manager - technical & derivative research, Angel One. Views expressed are his own. Readers' discretion is advised.
 

Nifty tech view

 
The Indian equity markets witnessed a spectacular week, with benchmark indices extending their upward trajectory. The Nifty50 commenced the week on a relatively subdued note, but buying momentum gathered significant traction during the final couple of sessions, propelling the index towards the 25800 mark. The rally was further reinforced by broad-based market participation, with high-beta counters and heavyweight banking stocks providing a meaningful impetus. Notably, the Bank Nifty emerged as a key outperformer, amplifying the positive market undertone. Consequently, the Nifty50 concluded the week firmly around the 25800 zone, registering an impressive weekly gain of 2.61 per cent.
 
 
A notable feature of the recent rally has been the Indian markets' resilience and continued decoupling from global peers, supported by sustained liquidity inflows from FIIs. Meanwhile, visible sectoral rotation has kept market participants engaged, creating opportunities across multiple pockets of the market. 
 
From a technical perspective, the decisive breakout above the 78.6% Fibonacci retracement level triggered fresh buying interest, with the bulls sustaining their dominance despite the approaching weekend and monthly expiry. The underlying structure remains firmly constructive, although the sharp upmove has pushed several technical and derivative parameters into overheated territory, warranting heightened caution.
 
On the levels front, the psychological 26,000 mark now emerges as the immediate milestone, followed by the previous lifetime high of 26,373, which could come into focus if the prevailing momentum sustains. On the downside, the 25,500-25,450 subzones have developed into a formidable support base, reinforced by substantial PE writing, and is expected to cushion any intermittent profit booking. Accordingly, the broader directional bias remains bullish, although a measured approach is warranted given the stretched momentum indicators and the upcoming truncated trading and monthly expiry week.
 
Going forward, the relentless outperformance of the Bank Nifty, coupled with persistent sectoral rotation, is likely to offer selective opportunities for traders. We recommend maintaining a stock-centric approach and focusing on thematic outperformers rather than aggressively chasing the extended rally in benchmark indices. Given the market conditions, disciplined exposure, stringent risk management and selective participation should remain paramount in the upcoming week.

data.title: SCO issues Indraprastha Communique, calls for respect for all civilisations
data.description:
The SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum hosted by India on Sunday came out with an outcome document -- Indraprastha Communique -- which called for the protection of cultural heritage, including from illicit trafficking, and "respecting every civilisation as an equal voice".

The three-day forum at the Purana Qila was inaugurated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on November 20. It saw the participation of delegates from various Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) member countries, including Pakistan's federal minister Musadik Malik.

The Communique begins with a text: "Member States and Dialogue Partners of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), assembled at 'Purana Qila' in New Delhi for the First SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, having held harmonious, constructive and meaningful deliberations".

 

It further says that they are cognisant that societies of the SCO countries have been shaped by centuries of interaction, exchange of ideas, movement of people, and sharing of knowledge, while "preserving their distinct identities, cultures, traditions and beliefs".

The Communique is named after the ancient moniker of the region where the Purana Qila is situated.

Member States and Dialogue Partners of the SCO in the outcome document have reaffirmed their collective commitment, founded on "mutual trust, harmony, equality, consultation, and respect for civilisational diversity and pursuit of sustainable development", and guided by these principles, "culture was recognised as a vital bridge of friendship and good-neighbourliness among the nations", and an important dimension of cooperation envisaged under the SCO Charter.

The Communique also recognised that cultural heritage encompasses monuments, manuscripts, literature, works of art, living traditions, cuisine, performing arts, creative endeavours and knowledge-systems passed on through generations.

Union Culture Secretary Vivek Aggarwal read the Communique at the closing session of the Forum which was hosted by the Ministry of Culture and the Ministry of External Affairs from November 20-22, with Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA) as the knowledge partner.

Asked how will the vision laid out in the document will be translated into action, Aggarwal said the SCO has a permanent Secretariat, and the Communique will be shared with the Secretariat. Then any action will be taken in conjunction with the SCO, he said.

Asked if there was concurrence of all members, the secretary said, it is "not exactly a negotiated document, it is an outcome document", which is an outcome of this Forum, and lays a "roadmap for future course of action".

The SCO Forum document also called for protection of heritage, including cultural properties from illicit trafficking, and from natural calamities.

The Communique also advocated embracing technology and "constructive use of artificial intelligence" in accessing cultural heritage.

It also affirmed "respecting every civilisation as an equal voice, and acknowledging its identity and contribution to humanity".

It recognised shared legacies in architecture, music, cuisine and textiles.

The Communique also underlined joint nomination by countries for UNESCO heritage tag.

Asked if the subject of joint nomination came up for discussions during the forum, including from Pakistan side, Aggarwal said, "As a principle, it has been discussed, but which countries will join, what nomination will be taken up, that will depend on future discussions that will happen".

Asked if the Communique was equivalent to a joint statement, and if there was concurrence of all members, Alok Dimri, Additional Secretary, Ministry of External Affairs, and National Coordinator for the SCO, said, "It's a matter of technicality, as this is an SCO event, but we have dialogue partners also participating. So, in SCO parlance, typically a joint statement is done by member states. But, nonetheless, it encapsulates the proceedings, and codifies it in the form a document." Asked why the name Indraprastha was chosen for the Communique, Aggarwal said, "The name of the place, where we are sitting, is known as 'Indraprast' in the revenue records also of Delhi. We have shown an artifact here carrying an inscription which mentions 'Indraprastha'".

The SCO was founded at a summit in Shanghai in 2001 by the presidents of Russia, China, the Kyrgyz Republic, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.

India and Pakistan became its permanent members in 2017. Iran became a member in 2023.

Scholars, academics, experts and cultural representatives gathered for the three-day event to explore the "shared civilisational heritage of SCO countries".

The initiative builds upon the proposal made by PM Modi at the SCO Summit in Tianjin, China, in 2025 to establish a dedicated platform for civilisational dialogue under the SCO framework. The proposal was subsequently welcomed in the Bishkek Declaration of the SCO.

After inaugurating the first SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum, Prime Minister Modi had emphasised the significance of holding a dialogue on civilisational connections in India at a time when global discussions are "dominated by war and unrest", asserting that cultural connections serve as the "strongest guarantee" for world peace.

In his address, he also noted that cultural and civilisational cooperation among member countries of the SCO can further strengthen these ties.

data.title: Democrats clinch biggest House majority since 1992 with at least 258 seats
data.description:
House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump's first midterm in 2018.

The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.

 

Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.

The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.

The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt-era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.

It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.

"Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure," said Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a former Army Ranger.

"There are people dying in this country and people losing their healthcare, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorized from ICE," he said at the Capitol, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "If you don't feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don't belong under this Capitol dome." Election rout creates a mandate to governThe numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump.

Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.

The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.

Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.

"This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., at the Capitol.

She called the big numbers "a mandate for change." Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.

"Everything should be tied back to the people - and how it's affecting the people," he said.

For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?" The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations - a standard oversight function of Congress - may amount to "blatant criminality." A new generation of leadersAfter House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow 218-214 Republican majority - meaning any few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda - the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.

Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.

"We're not a monolith - people come to the caucus with different ideas - it's OK," said Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.

Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.

"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families," Jordan said.

The GOP's highwater marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

data.title: OpenAI's chief scientist proposes industry limits on AI development
data.description:
By Jorgelina do Rosario
 
OpenAI’s chief scientist proposed that artificial intelligence companies agree to limits on developing increasingly powerful models until researchers have better ways to understand and monitor their behavior.
 
Jakub Pachocki called for industrywide standards that would establish thresholds for AI development, with companies agreeing not to exceed them until specific safety requirements are met, according to a post published Sunday.
 
“I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone,” Pachocki wrote.
 
The proposed limits could be based partly on a technical measurement known as perplexity, which gauges how well an AI model predicts the next piece of text. Pachocki didn’t specify what the initial limit should be or when it might take effect.
 
 
Pachocki warned that AI could accelerate advances in its own development as soon as 2027, potentially outpacing improvements in researchers’ ability to monitor and understand the technology.
 
OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman endorsed the proposal, calling Pachocki’s essay “the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile.” He said in a post on X that agreeing to common limits would help ensure “safety and control.”
 
The proposal comes as the US prepares for renewed debate over AI regulation following Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections. The party’s gains in the House, Senate and governors’ races could bring greater congressional scrutiny of technology companies and renewed efforts to establish AI safety rules.
 
Some lawmakers are also discussing the creation of a dedicated Senate committee to coordinate AI policy. President Donald Trump has opposed broad restrictions on AI development, setting up a potential clash with the incoming Democratic Congress over how to regulate the technology.

data.title: RBI Act may show the way on Tata Sons listing amid regulatory uncertainty
data.description:
Will the shareholders of Tata Sons, the holding company of the salt-to-software conglomerate, have the final say on the company’s proposed stock exchange listing, or will the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) mandate on compulsory listing prevail? Domain experts are scanning the RBI Act, which was enacted in 1934 and amended several times thereafter, to find an answer to that question, which is at the centre of the biggest corporate battle of the time.
 
Even as an amendment of the Articles of Association (AoA) of Tata Sons in the case of listing would require a special resolution passed by at least 75 per cent shareholders, sources believe listing is “imminent”. One of the sources, without wanting to be quoted, pointed at the sequence of events and also the various clauses of the RBI Act to state that non-compliance with directions of the central bank could have civil and criminal implications for the business of the company and its management. He added that the impact could be felt by the entire Tata group, and not just Tata Sons.
 
The forthcoming board meeting of Tata Sons on November 26 is expected to take up the company’s listing proposal. Some board members may assert that non-compliance with the RBI direction is not possible. Tata Trusts Chairman and Nominee Director Noel Tata has, however, already said that the alternative plan to restructure Tata Sons — so that it can remain private — would have to be discussed at the meeting.
 
The RBI identified Tata Sons as an upper layer non-banking financial company (NBFC) in 2022, after which, the company paid off all its debts and applied for deregistration as a core investment company in 2024. On September 11, 2026, the banking regulator rejected the Tata Sons application, while asking it to comply immediately. On November 16, 2026, it reiterated that the company must list, as is required of an upper layer NBFC. 
 
The RBI Act, ranging from Section 45 to Section 58, mentions the consequences of non-compliance, according to a domain expert. For instance, the regulator may cancel the certificate of registration (CoR), after providing a reasonable opportunity of hearing. Carrying on with business as an NBFC without the certificate of registration is an offence with imprisonment and financial penalty provisions.
 
There could be curbs on dealing with assets due to non-compliance with RBI directive. For an investment holding company, this could freeze divestments, block sales, stake dilutions and pledges across the group.
 
There’s a provision for removal of directors also to ensure financial stability or securing proper management in the public interest. According to a source, in Tata Son’s case, “public interest” and “proper management” are important clauses, and could affect any director where the relevant clause is applicable. Supersession of the board of directors for up to five years can be enforced as well for these reasons.
 
Under the RBI Act, imprisonment for a term of up to three years can also be given to persons in charge of and responsible for the conduct of business.
 
Sonam Chandwani, managing partner at KS Legal & Associates, told Business Standard that shareholders may decide whether they want the company to remain private, but the decision on its regulatory status rests with the RBI. “Shareholders cannot override or dilute the RBI’s independent regulatory mandate,” she said. As for the alternative plan mooted by Noel Tata, the RBI would have to examine the business post-restructuring before reconsidering its classification, Chandwani explained.  
 
“I do not think the RBI will resort to any harsh or punitive action against Tata Sons at this stage. The regulator’s approach is likely to be continued engagement, with discussions between the RBI and the management ongoing, persuading the latter to make a decision on compliance,’’ said Abizer Diwanji, founder, NeoStrat Advisors. Tata Sons may also point out that listing cannot happen overnight and would require time, including discussions with shareholders on a proposed plan, he said. “If the matter reaches serious confrontation, the ultimate recourse could ultimately be judicial, leaving the question of the RBI’s interpretation and jurisdiction to the courts.” But the management is expected to remain responsive to RBI’s concerns, he said.  
 
The RBI did not respond to a query from Business Standard on the matter.

data.title: India's armed forces turn to startups to build battlefield tech at speed
data.description:
India’s armed forces are turning to domestic startups for technology that can be developed and deployed quickly during conflicts, ranging from firefighting robots and underwater vision cameras to autonomous underwater vehicles.
 
At the Bengaluru Tech Summit, officials from the Army, Navy, Air Force, and iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence), the Department of Defence Production’s innovation initiative, said closer industry collaboration, co-development, and funding support could help address gaps in manufacturing, artificial intelligence (AI), and technology sovereignty.
 
A key challenge for startups is moving from working prototypes to large-scale production. Officials also stressed that human oversight must remain central to defence AI.
 
India spent $92.1 billion on its military in 2025, up 8.9 per cent from 2024, making it the world’s fifth-largest military spender, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
 
The institute credited the rise partly to the May 2025 conflict with Pakistan, which involved combat aircraft, drones, and missiles.
 
“Our role has changed from interacting with or purchasing equipment to co-developing with startups and industries,” said Wing Commander Gaddam Sandeep, commanding officer of the Regional Aerospace Innovation Division in Bengaluru.
 
Beyond the prototype
 
Vipin Yadav, deputy programme director at iDEX, said India’s defence startup ecosystem faces a gap between technology readiness and the ability to manufacture products at scale. “When we are ready for a product, it doesn’t mean we will be able to deliver it in huge numbers,” he said.
 
iDEX provides grants to early-stage startups and offers minimum pilot order quantities to give them visibility on potential orders after product validation. It has also introduced measures to help startups build business cases and secure repeat orders.
 
Grants alone may not be enough to establish production lines, said Commodore S K Singh, officer in charge of the Indian Navy’s Technology Development Acceleration Cell, which identifies capability gaps and works with startups to address them.
 
Under the Defence Acquisition Procedure, startups working with iDEX and the Technology Development Fund, with cumulative contract values of up to ₹250 crore, can access incentives including using intellectual property as collateral, advances of up to 15 per cent of the base contract value, and payments covering 100 per cent of raw material costs against invoices or committed purchases. They may also receive exemptions from liquidated damages.
 
The armed forces do not prevent startups from selling dual-use products commercially, Singh said. He cited a firefighting robot developed with a ₹1.5 crore grant that has since secured orders from the Army, Navy, Air Force, and oil and gas companies.
 
Co-development can also expand a product’s capabilities. The Navy initially approached a startup to build an AI-powered underwater vision camera for visibility in turbid waters. The project later expanded to include an echo sounder, sonar, and metal detector. The Navy inducted the integrated system, which Singh described as world-class. The startup subsequently adapted the technology for an autonomous underwater vehicle, enabling persistent underwater operations.
 
The Navy is working with around 150 startups, more than 30 of them in Bengaluru, Singh said. Sandeep said Karnataka accounts for more than 65 per cent of India's aerospace and AI industries. He called for centralised testing facilities and a hub-and-spoke model connecting startups with established aerospace companies.
 
AI built for the front lines
 
“The focus should not be on building larger AI models. It should be more on application-based small models which can help services in decision-making and surveillance,” Yadav said.
 
Sandeep said defence AI must evolve beyond prototypes because battlefield conditions and enemy tactics keep changing. Models need rapid iterations and testing in extreme temperatures and actual operational environments. “We don’t want huge computational models. We want small models, but it needs to have iterations faster,” he said.
 
The Navy needs task-specific models that can operate with limited data, power, and computing capacity, Singh said. Ships have restricted bandwidth when communicating with shore stations and can remain on patrol for two to three months, making frequent software updates difficult. The Navy therefore wants systems that can process data at the edge and detect rare events after long periods of inactivity.
 
Sandeep urged startups entering aviation to begin by modernising the Air Force’s legacy systems, some of which are 30 to 40 years old. They must also be prepared to maintain and support products throughout their 30-40-year service life.
 
Who owns the battlefield brain?
 
Access to classified data remains another challenge. Singh said the Navy wants developers to work alongside its personnel at naval facilities. Sandeep said the Air Force could share open-source and legacy data during development, but classified data would remain with the service once a model enters the defence domain. Further development would take place in a sandbox environment.
 
Lieutenant Colonel Sumanto Lahiri, officer in charge of the Indian Army Cell at the Army Design Bureau, said indigenous computing capabilities were essential to technology sovereignty. “Nobody is stopping us from developing our own sovereign software stacks,” he said.
 
The Navy has also launched a sovereign AI challenge through iDEX, requiring participating companies to transfer intellectual property rights and software to the service. The challenge attracted 68 industry proposals, Singh said.
 
Humans hold the trigger
 
Officials said AI would not replace human accountability in military operations. Lahiri said the Army had no scope for fully autonomous, AI-driven decision-making. “It is always human in the loop. The final call is taken by the human,” he said.
 
Singh said AI could independently support observation and surveillance, but human oversight would remain necessary for decisions and actions until the Navy developed sufficient confidence in the technology.
 
“AI is just an enabler. It’s not a decision maker,” Sandeep said. 
Building India’s next-gen arsenal
 
  • Firefighting robots, underwater vision systems, autonomous vehicles move into military’s tech pipeline
  • Scaling prototypes into mass production remains a key battle for defence startups
  • Military seeks lean, task-specific AI models for battlefield conditions
  • Indigenous computing, sovereign software emerge as critical lines of defence
  • AI may scan the battlefield, but humans control military decisions

data.title: Outdoor workers in Delhi bear pollution's cost amid GRAP restrictions
data.description:
Delhi’s air pollution crisis is taking a heavy toll on outdoor workers whose livelihoods depend on spending long hours on the road. As the national capital remains shrouded in smoke and dust amid elevated pollution levels, outdoor workers have no walls or air purifiers to shield them from toxic air.
 
The suspension of construction activities under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) from time to time leaves thousands of daily-wage construction workers without livelihoods and, in some cases, shelter. Migrant workers living at construction sites are forced to leave when work stops, workers’ representatives said.
 
“With the application of GRAP, all construction activities are now closed. The biggest impact is outright unemployment for these workers. They are day-to-day earners, so this leaves them without any income,” said Subhash Bhatnagar, coordinator of the National Campaign Committee for Central Legislation on Construction Labour.
 
Restrictions on non-essential construction and demolition activities, including earthwork, trenching, road construction, and major repairs, are covered under Stage III of GRAP. These restrictions were revoked on November 17 after around 10 days of implementation across Delhi-National Capital Region. However, with pollution remaining a  problem, there is no guarantee that the restrictions will not return as winter progresses.
 
The October 30 order restricting dust-generating demolition and outdoor construction activities would remain in force, the Commission for Air Quality Management said. The impact is particularly severe for migrant workers who live at construction sites and depend on contractors for accommodation. While some turn to rickshaw driving or loading and unloading work at mandis, these options are already saturated. Finding work at mandis also requires contacts, which migrant workers often lack, Bhatnagar said. “Workers are not only left jobless, but also homeless,” he said.
 
He said unions were unable to negotiate alternative accommodation with contractors or authorities because they were not allowed to enter construction sites. Many construction workers also remain outside the welfare system because of limited awareness and access to registration.  
 
Delhi has an estimated 1.2 million construction workers, but official records account for only 300,000-400,000, Bhatnagar said.
 
Nationally, nearly 120 million construction workers were estimated to be employed, of whom around 70 million were registered with welfare boards, he said. He added that no workers had received compensation from the welfare board so far this year.
 
A report published last year by Greenpeace India, an environmental non-profit campaigning network, noted that Delhi alone is home to over 400,000 street vendors, an estimated 200,000 waste pickers, around 500,000 domestic workers and 500,000 rickshaw pullers.
 
“These workers often endure long hours outdoors without access to basic infrastructure such as clean water, cooling spaces, sanitation, or shelter, making them acutely vulnerable to the worsening impacts of climate change,” it stated.
 
“Around 80 per cent of Delhi’s workforce, including 82 per cent of working men and 76 per cent of working women, are employed in the informal sector.” Gig workers who spend 10-11 hours on the road have reported burning eyes, sore throats, breathlessness, and persistent coughs amid worsening pollution, said Nitesh Kumar Das, organising secretary of the Gig Workers Association (GigWA).
 
“For most workers, cutting down work hours is not a real choice. If they log off, they earn less, lose their incentives, and sometimes get penalised. Even one or two days offline can hurt their income badly,” Das said. He added that companies did not provide workers with protective equipment such as masks, leaving them to purchase these at their own expense.
 
In the short term, fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and toxic gases can trigger persistent coughing, throat irritation, breathlessness, headaches, eye irritation, and worsening asthma, said Dr Pritpal Kaur, senior consultant in pulmonology at Delhi’s Apollo Spectra Hospital.
 
“Prolonged exposure can cause chronic inflammation in the lungs, reduced lung function, and increased susceptibility to respiratory infections,” Kaur said. “Over time, these workers face a higher risk of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), cardiovascular disease, stroke, and lung cancer. Continuous exposure without adequate protection makes cumulative health damage particularly concerning.”
 
Kaur said reports of respiratory complaints were rising across Delhi as air pollution worsened. Hospitals were reporting patients with persistent coughs, wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and aggravated asthma or COPD.
 
“Some facilities have reported substantial increases in respiratory consultations, although the rise varies between hospitals,” she said. “Outdoor workers are particularly vulnerable because prolonged exposure can aggravate existing respiratory conditions and trigger symptoms even in previously healthy individuals. However, worker-specific hospitalisation data remains limited.”
 
The growing number of pollution-related consultations highlights the need for early diagnosis, respiratory screening, and preventive measures, especially among individuals exposed to polluted air throughout their working hours, Kaur said.
 
Das cited the case of a woman worker who returned to work despite a serious chest infection after spending nearly ₹3,000 on medicines over seven days. Another woman carried her three-year-old child on her back while making deliveries. Both developed severe coughs as pollution worsened.
 
“Workers usually stop only when they fall sick, and then they suffer twice,” Das said, adding that workers often delayed or skipped medical treatment because taking time off meant losing daily earnings.
 
“At the very least, they need free masks, rest stops with clean air, medical support when they fall ill, and extra pay on days when the air is at its worst,” he said.

data.title: 500 mn lifted out of poverty, but some still hesitate to acknowledge it: PM
data.description:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Sunday said some individuals still hesitate to acknowledge that 50 crore people have been pulled out of poverty in the country, in an apparent dig at the Opposition.
 
Addressing BJP workers virtually during a post-Diwali 'Sneh Milan' programme organised across all 182 assembly constituencies in Gujarat, he said the achievement reflected the success of his government's policies and efforts.
 
"All those who sacrificed their lives for independence, all those who dedicated their lives to freedom, all those who spent their youth in jails for independence, wherever their souls may be, today they must be the happiest seeing this World Bank report, thinking, 'finally, poverty is leaving my country'," he said.
 
 
According to a World Bank report, India's extreme poverty rate dropped sharply to 2.6 per cent in 2023 from 27.1 per cent in 2011, with the country lifting an estimated 496 million people out of poverty.
 
"A thousand years of slavery had impoverished us; for the first time after a thousand years of slavery, 50 crore people are coming out of poverty. There can be no greater satisfaction in life than this, no greater achievement than this," Modi said.
 
However, he said some people were still reluctant to acknowledge the achievement.
 
"I know many people still hesitate to say this aloud, because all of this happened during this period (BJP rule). They don't like it. Whether they like it or not, we have the satisfaction that our efforts have borne fruit," Modi said.
 
Terming the development the beginning of a new chapter in the lives of citizens, he said coming generations would witness the country's "golden era".
 
"Our intention is true, our policy is right, our direction is right, and there is no shortcoming in our hard work," he said.
 
The BJP had organised the programme across all 182 assembly constituencies in Gujarat. Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel listened to the PM's virtual address in his Ghatlodia constituency.
 
Modi said this year's Diwali was significant for him as it marked 25 years since he became Gujarat's chief minister in October 2001.
 
He credited generations of BJP workers for supporting him in his political journey and said their hard work had enabled him to serve his home state and the country.
 
Recalling the devastating 2001 Gujarat earthquake, Modi said his first Diwali as chief minister was spent with affected families.
 
"That day, my belief became very strong that the true happiness of festivals, the true joy of festivals, lies in lighting a lamp of hope in someone else's life," he said.
 
Modi said the spirit of public participation had helped Gujarat overcome the devastation and transform Kutch into a new centre of hope. The reconstruction efforts subsequently spread across the state, leading to a wider transformation, he said.
 
Recalling Gujarat's development journey, Modi said the state, once largely associated with trade, had expanded its presence in sectors such as agriculture, dairy, industries, semiconductors, petrochemicals, automobiles and green energy.
 
He said Gujarat's economic progress had contributed significantly to the country's development and reiterated his earlier slogan of achieving national development through Gujarat's development.
 
Recalling the difficult years around 2001, he said party workers had gone door-to-door collecting 'sukhdi' (a traditional sweet) for poor families to provide them with essential nutrition. They had also arranged cattle fodder from different parts of the country during droughts and organised cattle camps, he said.
 
The PM said public participation had helped Gujarat overcome droughts and water shortages.
 
"Campaigns to conserve water and construct check dams had gradually turned into mass movements, changing the situation in the state," he said.
 
The prime minister also referred to the Garib Kalyan Melas launched during his tenure as chief minister in 2001, saying they helped build confidence among poor families and encouraged them to come out of poverty.
 
"The experience gained from launching such programmes helped me create welfare schemes introduced by my government at the Centre after 2014," Modi said.
 
Modi recalled that when his government started opening bank accounts for the poor, critics questioned their utility, while similar doubts were raised over the provision of LPG connections to households that could not afford cylinder refills.
 
"We kept making scheme after scheme and taking them to the last person in the queue. We proved what social justice means for those who are rightful claimants and in need. And who were the ones without bank accounts? Our Dalit families, tribal families, the oppressed and downtrodden, as well as the women," the PM said.
 
While bank accounts were opened, gas stoves arrived in homes, and electricity connections and Ayushman cards were distributed to the needy, he said.
 
"As a result of all these schemes, 50 crore people have come out of poverty," the PM added.
 
Modi urged BJP workers to keep national interest above party interests. He said the social harmony and unity developed in Gujarat would help the state and the country progress.
 
He expressed confidence that Gujarat would achieve much more in the next 20 years than it had accomplished over the previous 25 years.

data.title: To list or not to list: Noel Tata wants Tata Sons Nov 26 board meet deferred
data.description:
Tata Trusts chairman and nominee director on the Tata Sons board, Noel Tata, is learnt to have asked the group's holding company to defer the board meeting scheduled for November 26. The board agenda was uploaded over the weekend, with less than a week to go before the meeting. Tata Sons is expected to defer the board meeting, and a fresh date will be decided soon.
 
The next board meeting, the first after the September 17 face-off between the Tata Sons directors and Noel Tata, is likely to be stormy as well. The proposed listing of Tata Sons would come up at the next board meeting amid opposition from Noel, it is learnt. The discussion assumes greater significance against the backdrop of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) reiterating that listing is mandatory for Tata Sons as an upper-layer non-banking financial company (NBFC).
 
 
Noel Tata, in a recent letter, has maintained that the alternative plan to keep Tata Sons private must be discussed at the upcoming board meeting. The plan, mooted by Noel, involves merging two group operating companies — Tata Electronics Systems Solutions (TESS) and Tata Consulting Engineers (TCE) — into Tata Sons so that the company does not qualify as a core investment company or an upper-layer NBFC.
 
While any listing proposal has to go to shareholders for their approval, experts believe that shareholders cannot override or dilute regulatory compliance. Clarity on this front is likely to emerge in a few days after the next board meeting. The RBI had classified Tata Sons as an upper-layer NBFC in 2022, giving it three years to comply — that is, mandatorily go for a stock market listing. However, Tata Sons cleared its debt and applied to deregister from the core investment company (CIC) category in 2024. In September 2026, the RBI rejected Tata Sons' application, asking it to comply with its directive immediately. Then, in November 2026, it again reiterated that Tata Sons must list.
 
On September 17, the Tata Sons board meeting had turned into a boardroom battle, with all directors other than Noel backing a third term for N Chandrasekaran as executive chairman of the company. In the voting that followed, two nominee directors — Noel Tata and Venu Srinivasan — went against each other, resulting in a casting vote by independent director Harish Manwani, who was chairing the discussion. The listing of Tata Sons was not put to a vote, but the entire board, other than Noel, backed the proposal.
